items.title: Completing the square was a geometric procedure 4000 years ago
items.claim: Babylonians (~1800 BC) solved quadratic equations using cut-and-paste geometric procedures. They literally cut a square into pieces and rearranged them. The algebraic 'completing the square' technique is the algebraic shadow of this physical manipulation.

options.text: It is a modern algebraic trick

x squared + bx can be VISUALISED as a square (x by x) plus a rectangle (b by x); cutting the rectangle in half and attaching each half to the square's adjacent sides produces an L-shape. Completing the missing corner adds (b/2) squared and gives a complete square of side (x + b/2)
It only works for special quadratics

items.reveal_title: Geometric origin of the quadratic formula
items.reveal:
Old Babylonian tablets (YBC 7289, c. 1800 BC) show problems like: 'I added the side of a square to its area and got 0.75. What is the side?'

The procedure: take half of 1 (the coefficient of the side) — that's 0.5. Square it — 0.25. Add to 0.75 — that's 1. Square root of 1 is 1. Subtract 0.5 — answer is 0.5.

What they were doing geometrically: visualise x^2 (a square) + x (a rectangle, 1 by x). Cut the rectangle in half (each piece is 1/2 by x). Attach one piece to each adjacent side of the square. You now have an L-shape with side (x + 1/2). Fill in the missing corner (1/2 by 1/2 = 1/4). Total area is x^2 + x + 1/4 = (x + 1/2)^2.

From x^2 + x = 0.75, add 1/4 to both sides: (x + 1/2)^2 = 1, so x + 1/2 = 1, x = 0.5.

The quadratic formula x = (-b plus/minus sqrt(b^2 - 4ac))/(2a) is this same procedure for ax^2 + bx + c = 0, fully generalised. Al-Khwarizmi (Baghdad, c. 825) gave the systematic algebraic version. The word 'algebra' comes from his treatise's title — 'al-jabr' meaning 'completion' or 'restoration', literally 'reassembling broken parts'.

Geometric algebra: an entire branch of mathematics treats algebraic identities as geometric statements. Many people find quadratics easier to remember when they can VISUALISE the completed square.
items.why: Quadratic formulas feel like magic algebra. They are the algebraic encoding of a physical cut-and-rearrange procedure that has been used for 4000 years.

items.title: Some quadratics never touch zero — and you can prove it in one step
items.claim: x^2 + 2x + 5: positive for every real x. The graph never reaches zero. You don't need calculus or graph-plotting — you can see this in one rearrangement.

options.text: Complete the square: x^2 + 2x + 5 = (x + 1)^2 + 4. The first term is non-negative; adding 4 means the whole expression is at least 4. Never zero
It cannot be proved without calculus

items.reveal:
For ax^2 + bx + c with a > 0, the discriminant b^2 - 4ac determines:
- Discriminant > 0: two real roots; graph crosses x-axis twice.
- Discriminant = 0: one repeated real root; graph touches x-axis.
- Discriminant < 0: no real roots; graph stays entirely above x-axis (if a > 0) or below (if a < 0).

x^2 + 2x + 5: a = 1, b = 2, c = 5. Discriminant = 4 - 20 = -16 < 0. No real roots.

Completing the square gives a stronger statement: the MINIMUM value of the quadratic. (x + 1)^2 + 4 has minimum 4 when x = -1. So x^2 + 2x + 5 is always at least 4.

General quadratic ax^2 + bx + c = a(x + b/(2a))^2 + (c - b^2/(4a)). Minimum value (for a > 0) is c - b^2/(4a) = -(b^2 - 4ac)/(4a) — same expression as the discriminant.

Applications:
- Optimisation: many minimisation problems reduce to completing the square.
- Inequality proofs: AM-GM and Cauchy-Schwarz often pivot on quadratic positivity.
- Definite matrices: a quadratic form x^T M x > 0 for all non-zero x means M is positive definite — central to optimisation and statistics.
items.why: Quadratics feel like they should always cross zero somewhere. Many don't. The discriminant settles which ones, and completing the square exposes the minimum directly — without calculus.

items.title: A university that favoured women overall was sued for discriminating against them
items.claim: Berkeley's graduate admissions, 1973: men admitted at 44%, women at 35%. Looks like discrimination. Break it down by department — and in most departments, women were admitted at HIGHER rates. The overall trend reverses when disaggregated.
items.prompt: How can the parts and the whole point opposite ways?

options.text: Simpson's paradox: women applied disproportionately to highly competitive departments with low admission rates for everyone; the overall ratio is dominated by where applicants applied, not how each department treated them
Only one of the figures is true

items.reveal_title: Simpson's paradox in real admissions data
items.reveal:
Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell (Science 1975) analysed Berkeley's 1973 fall admissions. Aggregate: 44% of male applicants admitted vs 35% of female. Looks like a 9-point bias.

Department-by-department: of the 6 largest departments, 4 actually favoured women (higher admission rate). Only 2 favoured men.

What's going on: women disproportionately applied to humanities and social sciences (low admission rates for everyone, ~5-30%). Men disproportionately applied to physics, engineering, etc. (higher admission rates, ~50-70%). The aggregate bias against women was driven by their CHOICE of department, not by departmental policies.

The pattern is named after Edward H. Simpson (1951 statistician), though Pearson and Yule had noted it earlier.

The lesson: aggregating data across groups can REVERSE the direction of a trend present in every group. Whenever you see a aggregate correlation in observational data, ask whether breaking it down by relevant subgroup changes the story.

Real-world examples: kidney stone treatment effectiveness, racial sentencing disparities, COVID death rates by age, batting averages across seasons.
items.why: Aggregate statistics feel definitive. Disaggregating by a confounder can reverse the apparent trend — sometimes drastically. The same data tell different stories at different levels.
